facts.claim: "Slowly (Acoustic)" is a one-track single by Skuff Micksun, released January 13, 2023, with a running time of 2:43 and a ℗ line to 652534 Records DK.
Qobuz's credits for the Slowly listing (released 13/01/2023 on 652534 Records DK) name Casey W. Skufca as composer and lyricist and Tyler Cratcha as composer. Skuff Micksun is the main artist.
The original studio version, "Slowly", came out August 5, 2022 on the artist's Bandcamp. The acoustic version followed as a separate single.
The artist announced the acoustic version on TikTok with the line "Slowly acoustic is out everywhere to keep you warm!" and tagged it #acoustic #singersongwriter #midwestemo #emo.
Skuff Micksun's limited-edition signed and numbered pink vinyl (200 copies) includes "Slowly (Acoustic)" on Side A, after "Magnificent".
Skuff Micksun is based in Cleveland, Ohio.

He started playing music at 13 on a self-taught guitar. He played in Cleveland bands until 19, then moved to Chicago and dropped out of Columbia after one year. He spent about six years there in a band while writing the solo project that became Skuff Micksun.
He added "Micksun" to his name to honor his father, Mick, who died in 2009.
Press notes describe him as an alternative/indie artist from Cleveland who quit a 9-to-5 to become a full-time artist, and who combines spoken word with melodies.
Before music became his full-time work, his jobs included muralist, tattoo artist, graphic designer, children's art teacher, set construction worker and art director.

research.lineage: Sources place him in the Cleveland, Ohio underground as an alternative/indie singer-songwriter who blends spoken-word poetry with acoustic, folk and electronic touches, and he tags his own acoustic material #midwestemo.

draft:
**Slowly** starts with someone waking up and checking whether he's dead. "Born again out of REM," Skuff Micksun sings, then lists the morning chores of getting through: drag the body out of bed, and "Tell myself I'm okay." The next line is "then proceed with my day," and the flatness is the point. It's a routine, not a recovery. The words "mostly lonely" hang there on their own, the one thing the routine can't cover.

The song keeps sliding between "I" and "we." "We don't wanna be dark no more," it says, then "I don't wanna," as if the narrator can't decide whether this sinking feeling is shared or his alone. That uncertainty is the most human thing in the song. In the second verse the words speed into a run of rhymes: senses, senseless, headless, relentless, endless, wreck-less. This is where his habit of mixing spoken word with melody shows. The wordplay is almost a joke, until it turns into "It's all my fault" and then, right after, "We might all be doomed." Blaming himself and fearing for everyone sit next to each other with no line between them. Then comes the sharpest moment, a narrator catching himself mid-spiral: "Am I doing it again." He knows the pattern of getting "real, real dark" in his head and wanting out of his own skin. Knowing it doesn't stop it.

The chorus asks for very little, a light, a spark, a smile from someone that comes from a part of them that hasn't died. It's modest and generous at once. The narrator is looking for something alive in other people because he's short on it himself. Then it ends on "But I'm barely alive," and the hope doesn't cancel the confession.

This acoustic take came out in January 2023, after the studio original arrived on Bandcamp the previous August. Fingerpicked guitar gives way to strumming as a kick, snare and hi-hat come in, and a bass walks underneath. The tempo is medium and the groove is relaxed but pushing forward. The mix is clean and clear. Skuff Micksun's mid-range voice has a little rasp in it and stays conversational, with no harmonies dressing it up, so it sounds like someone talking you through a bad week. He tagged the release #midwestemo, and it fits that tradition's habit of putting a plain, unguarded confession over guitars that keep moving. When he announced it, he said it was out "to keep you warm," which is a kind way to frame a song this dark.

He wrote it with Tyler Cratcha, credited under his given name, Casey W. Skufca. He works out of Cleveland and has said the "Micksun" honors his late father, Mick. The chorus is plain to the point of feeling generic on first listen, and the "we" sometimes blurs who's actually in trouble. But that blur is also how depression talks.

What sticks is the narrator's voice catching itself, asking if it's happening again, and you recognizing that question from the inside.

factCheck.claim: Lyric quote "Born again out of REM" and the opening situation of waking up and contemplating being dead
factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics ("Contemplate if I'm dead").

factCheck.claim: "Tell myself I'm okay" and "then proceed with my day" quoted as lines
factCheck.note: The lines are in the lyrics, but the draft quoted far more than three lyric lines. These two are now paraphrased.

factCheck.claim: "Mostly lonely" hangs on its own
factCheck.note: It appears as a standalone line twice. Now paraphrased to stay within the three-quote limit.

factCheck.claim: Slides between "I" and "we" ("We don't wanna be dark no more" / "I don't wanna")
factCheck.note: The lyrics shift between we and I. Now paraphrased rather than quoted.

factCheck.claim: Second-verse run of words: senses, senseless, headless, relentless, endless, wreck-less
factCheck.note: All words appear in the lyrics. Reworded as a run of -less words, since senses/senseless isn't a true rhyme.

factCheck.claim: Spoken-word-with-melody habit shows in the wordplay
factCheck.note: Press notes say he combines spoken word with melodies. The link to this passage is interpretation.

factCheck.claim: "It's all my fault" followed directly by "We might all be doomed"
factCheck.note: The lines are consecutive in the lyrics. Now paraphrased.

factCheck.claim: "Am I doing it again" / getting "real, real dark" / wanting out of his own skin
factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics. "Am I doing it again" is kept as a quote; the other lines are paraphrased.

factCheck.claim: Chorus asks for a light, a spark, a smile from a part of someone that hasn't died
factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics.

factCheck.claim: "Then it ends on 'But I'm barely alive'"
factCheck.note: The quote matches the lyrics, but "ends" is a claim about song structure. Changed to the chorus landing on that line.

factCheck.claim: Acoustic take released January 2023; studio original on Bandcamp the previous August
factCheck.note: Released 2023-01-13; the original came out Aug 5, 2022 on Bandcamp.

factCheck.claim: Fingerpicked guitar gives way to strumming as kick, snare and hi-hat come in, with a walking bass
factCheck.note: Fingerpicked and strummed guitar, walking bass, and kick/snare/hi-hat are backed by two passes. The sequence of drums entering is a positional claim, and pass 3 describes a full band from the start, so it was dropped.

factCheck.claim: Medium tempo, relaxed but driving groove
factCheck.note: All passes agree on medium/moderate and relaxed. Two say driving.

factCheck.claim: Mix is clean and clear
factCheck.note: All three passes agree.

factCheck.claim: Mid-range voice with a little rasp, conversational, no harmonies
factCheck.note: Mid-range, conversational and no harmonies are backed by at least two passes. Rasp appears in only one pass, so it was removed.

factCheck.claim: He tagged the release #midwestemo
factCheck.note: He tagged the TikTok announcement, not the release itself.

factCheck.claim: It fits that tradition's habit of putting a plain, unguarded confession over guitars that keep moving

factCheck.claim: He said it was out "to keep you warm"
factCheck.note: From the TikTok announcement: "Slowly acoustic is out everywhere to keep you warm!"

factCheck.claim: He wrote it with Tyler Cratcha, credited under his given name, Casey W. Skufca
factCheck.note: Credits name Casey W. Skufca as composer and lyricist and Tyler Cratcha as composer. Nothing says Skufca is his given name or that he is the same person as Skuff Micksun, so that was removed.

factCheck.claim: Based in Cleveland; "Micksun" honors his late father, Mick
